title: Nanostack probe scripts and async trace adapter - experimental runbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a lightweight working runbook for the nanostack probe collection scripts and the async-trace-adapter shim. Goal: provide a fast way to collect aligned, low-noise traces across CPU and GPU stack boundaries for tail-latency investigations, and to be able to replay the same synthetic workload in CI. This doc is intentionally pragmatic: fragmentary notes, command snippets, and known pitfalls for on-call and performance engineers.

Scope and when to use this: 
- Use when a production or staging instance shows intermittent tail latency spikes (>95th percentile) and existing high-level metrics (p99 traces, opentelemetry spans) don't reveal the root cause.
- Use when you need to correlate kernel scheduling, user-space hotspots, and NVTX/GPU markers in a single timeline.
- Not intended for baseline throughput tuning (use bench scripts under tools/bench instead).

High-level approach:
1) Attach nanostack probes (small eBPF probes + user-space perf sampling) to the runtime process group. Probes are focused on: scheduler wakeups, futex waits, network socket wakes, and mmap/fork hotspots.
2) Run async-trace-adapter to collect trace fragments from microservices that are containerized with limited permissions (it performs a lightweight relay to an in-cluster collector).
3) Merge kernel timestamps, user-space perf samples, and NVTX/GPU events into a single chronology and generate a condensed timeline (CSV + HTML visualization).
4) Reproduce the event with the synthetic scenario builder to iterate quickly.

Components (what each script does):
- nanostack-attach.sh (bash): attaches eBPF uprobes and lightweight perf counters to a PID or cgroup. Keeps runfiles under /tmp/nanostack-<runid>/ and rotates every 10m.
  - flags: --pid, --cgroup, --duration, --rotate
  - output: perf.data.gz, bpf-events.log, nvtx.log
- async-trace-adapter.py (python): runs as a sidecar or locally with elevated perms. Listens on a unix socket for small JSON trace fragments from containers that cannot run perf. Adds an aligned kernel timestamp and forwards to collector.
  - config: adapter config lives in /etc/nanostack/adapter.yaml (socket path, retention, max-fragment-size)
- merge-timeline.go (golang): post-process merges perf.data (via perf script), BPF events, and NVTX event dumps into timeline.jsonl and a condensed CSV used by quickviz.html
- synthetic-replay.py: reproduces request patterns (kv-cache warmup steps, prefix caching, and bursty concurrent tail patterns). It can pin CPUs, vary sequence lengths, and control KV-cache hit rates.

Quickstart (collect a single 5 minute trace):
1) On staging host with sudo privileges:
   sudo ./nanostack-attach.sh --pid 4321 --duration 300 --rotate 0 
   (this will create /tmp/nanostack-<timestamp>/perf.data.gz and bpf-events.log)
2) Start adapter (if service is containerized without perf):
   sudo systemctl start nanostack-adapter  # installs a socket under /var/run/nanostack.sock
   OR run one-off: sudo python3 async-trace-adapter.py --socket /var/run/nanostack.sock --out /tmp/nanostack-<runid>/adapter.json
3) Trigger the workload that produces spikes (manual or synthetic-replay.py)
4) After collection, run merge step: ./merge-timeline --run /tmp/nanostack-<runid>/ --out /tmp/nanostack-<runid>/timeline.html
5) Open timeline.html and inspect: color legend maps: kernel-sched, user-hotspot, nvtx-start/stop, futex-wake.

Perf CI integration notes (experimental job):
- Job name: perf/trace-arcadia-nanostack
- Trigger: nightly on the 3 largest-instance-types + on PR labeled perf/trace-needed
- Steps: spin up minimal cluster, deploy runtime with trace-agent sidecar, run synthetic-replay with seeded random to produce deterministic sequence, collect merged timeline artifact.
- Artifacts: timeline.html (zipped), perf.data.gz, adapter.json, repro script output.
- Failure criteria: new p95 spike > baseline p95 * 1.25 or new kernel-sched wakeups per-request > baseline + 10
- Storage: keep last 30 runs in S3 for diffing and regression alerts.

Synthetic scenarios (how we reproduce the hard-to-hit spikes):
- KV-cache warmup + cold-spot injection: synthetic-replay has phases: 1) heavy warmup to populate prefix cache, 2) introduce rare prefix variations (1:1000) to force K/V misses, 3) concurrently open N clients to create scheduling pressure.
- Memory-fragmentation stress: pin process to CPU and do repeated mmap/munmap loops in a helper thread to observe user-kernel pagefault patterns.
- Mixed CPU/GPU burst: trigger a short NVTX-marked GPU inference task while simultaneously blocking a helper thread on a futex to see KV cache reclaim interactions.

Known pitfalls and gotchas:
- perf sampling rate: default 99Hz is too coarse; we recommend 997Hz for tail-latency work. But beware of overhead on small instances (monitor host load).
- eBPF maps can fill quickly in high-concurrency tests; adapter has a backpressure flag --drop-on-full that we use in CI to avoid OOMing host.
- Timestamps: clocksource mismatch between GPU NVTX and kernel timestamps causes ~1-4ms skew; merge-timeline applies a linear calibration step using a shared sync-point (we insert an nvtx sync event at collection start).
- Containerized collection: adding SYS_ADMIN to containers is unacceptable for prod; prefer sidecar adapter to avoid changing runtime containers.

Troubleshooting quick-reference:
- No NVTX events in timeline: ensure model runner compiled with NVTX_ENABLED=1 and exporter writes nvtx.log to shared memory path /dev/shm/nvtx-<pid>.
- perf binary missing: apt-get install linux-tools-common linux-tools-$(uname -r) on debian images, or use perf from our debug-builder image.
- BPF permission denied: check kernel v5.8+ and cap_sys_admin for attaching; privileged node required or use eBPF-based collection host.

Open questions / TODOs (short-running backlog):
- Add prometheus counters in adapter for dropped fragments (PR queued: runtime#852).
- Move merge-timeline to run as part of perf CI container rather than local dev machine. (Blocked by encoded NVTX schema parity).
- Investigate a tiny userspace tracer alternative that uses clock_gettime(CLOCK_MONOTONIC_COARSE) to avoid needing kernel probes for most scenarios.

References and change log:
- 2024-03-22: initial draft (Priya) with basic scripts and merge tool prototypes.
- 2024-04-11: added synthetic scenario builder and CI job notes (Marcus).

Links: runtime PRs and tickets included above. Slack thread: #perf-runtime (see thread: spike-2024-03-19 for initial incident notes).

If you use this doc: please copy to a new doc before editing and add yourself to collaborators. Mark "status: in_review" when you've validated adapter on staging.

Example commands (pasteable):
- Attach to cgroup (recommended): sudo ./nanostack-attach.sh --cgroup /sys/fs/cgroup/system.slice/runtime.service --duration 600
- Run adapter locally (dev): sudo PYTHONPATH=. python3 async-trace-adapter.py --socket /tmp/nano.sock --out ./out/adapter.json --verbose
- Merge artifacts: ./merge-timeline --run /tmp/nanostack-168000/ --out ./out/timeline.html --calibrate-sync nvtx

End of runbook.
